strengths: AutoSeg addresses a useful problem: semantic segmentation without requiring users to enumerate the relevant classes. Generating image-specific vocabularies could make existing open-vocabulary segmentors more practical.

BCC offers an interesting use of pretrained BLIP: decoding clustered subsets of patch embeddings to discover less salient objects, then supplying their names to a segmentation model without additional training.

The comparisons using the same X-Decoder backbone provide encouraging evidence. Table 1 reports improvements over plain BLIP captioning from 38.0 to 71.8 class-agnostic mIoU on VOC and from 35.3 to 47.7 on Context. Supplementary Table 4 includes useful SAM+BLIP and LLaVA alternatives.

The manuscript provides substantial implementation detail, evaluator prompts and pseudocode, and a code link. The supplementary failure cases meaningfully identify compound-noun parsing errors and competition between related class names.
weaknesses: The central evaluator, LAVE, is insufficiently validated. Appendix A relies on the LLM remembering the Context and ADE20K vocabularies instead of supplying the allowed labels. Its prompts also direct stuff descriptions to background, although these datasets and Cityscapes contain valid stuff classes; exact-name overrides do not resolve this for synonyms. No mapping-accuracy audit, human agreement study, or prompt/model sensitivity analysis establishes reliability. Moreover, mapping predictions into fixed categories cannot verify the correctness of the finer-grained names highlighted in the qualitative results.

The headline comparisons require a protocol audit. Table 3 labels its Context column PC-459, but entries such as X-Decoder's 65.1 and FC-CLIP's 58.4 appear to correspond to the 59-class benchmark. The paper also does not demonstrate that ZeroSeg was re-evaluated using LAVE, despite Section 3.4 describing its different mapping procedure. Consequently, the reported superiority can confound segmentation quality with label-set and evaluator differences.

Model selection and statistical reliability are unclear. Section 4.1 reports Bayesian optimization against VOC mIoU without identifying a separate tuning split, while Table 3 uses each dataset's best caption-cycle result from Table 2. Only validation-set evaluations are described. With stochastic caption generation and no repeated-run uncertainty, the 11.7 versus 11.4 Context advantage is particularly inconclusive.

The distinctive contribution is not sufficiently isolated. Guidance-free segmentation and text-free grounding are acknowledged prior settings, so the methodological case rests largely on BCC. The experiments do not separately ablate multiple resolutions, cluster alignment, positional features, CRF refinement, or majority filtering. Only X-Decoder is tested, and runtime is unreported despite repeated clustering and caption generation. These omissions limit conclusions about which components matter and how broadly useful the framework is.

Several specification issues hinder reproduction: Section 3.1 describes Hungarian matching, whereas Equation 9 defines independent maximum-IoU assignments, which need not produce the same correspondence. Cross-resolution alignment and the handling of concatenated positional features before the frozen BLIP decoder also need clarification. These are fixable presentation issues; evaluator validity and experimental comparability are the primary reasons for the recommendation.
